screens.title: Deployment and Security Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment is more than making code available; it's about releasing a reliable, secure application that interacts with real value. In this lesson you will learn how to move your Anchor program through devnet and testnet into mainnet-beta, how to update client configuration after a deploy, and how to protect the keys that control upgrades and ownership. We will emphasize practical steps: running anchor deploy, noting the new Program ID, updating the client PROGRAM_ID and connection endpoint, and validating behavior on a public explorer. Security is threaded through every step. You will see concrete recommendations for storing deployer keys, preferring hardware wallets or encrypted vaults, and the immediate actions to take if a key is exposed. Finally, we'll preview common vulnerabilities you must check for — reentrancy-like flows, signer and ownership checks, integer wrapping, and denial-of-service vectors — and how to adopt simple defensive patterns. By the end of the section you'll understand the deploy lifecycle and why careful key management and auditing are essential before going live.

screens.title: Solana Networks — Devnet, Testnet, Mainnet-beta
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the three public Solana clusters is essential to a safe deploy process. Devnet is the development playground: you can airdrop free SOL, iterate quickly, and accept that state can reset. Use it for daily development, quick client integration, and early user flows. Testnet is a more stable public network that better mirrors mainnet-beta behavior and uptime; use it for larger integration tests and load scenarios before a public release. Mainnet-beta is the production network where real value moves. Deploys here must be audited, your deployer key must be secured, and rollback or emergency plans should be ready. A common misconception is treating devnet tests as sufficient for production; devnet does not guarantee the same uptime or network conditions. Another subtle point: program IDs created by a local validator will differ from the ID produced by anchor deploy to a public cluster, so always note the Program ID printed after deploy and update your client. Example: you will typically develop and test on devnet, then run broader tests on testnet, and finally perform a controlled, phased roll-out to mainnet-beta. Ask yourself: have I tested scale and secured upgrade paths before mainnet?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Network Comparison
Cluster Comparison
Choose the right environment for each stage of release.
Devnet
Fast feedback, free airdrops, ephemeral state. Ideal for developer iteration and verifying client integration flow.
Testnet
Closer to production behavior with more stable uptime. Use it for stress testing and community betas.
Mainnet-beta
Real economic activity. Requires audits, monitoring, and secure key custody before deploying.
Practical checklist
Confirm anchor deploy target before deploying.
Use --provider.cluster to specify devnet/testnet/mainnet-beta.
Record the Program ID printed by anchor deploy.
Update client-side PROGRAM_ID and idl.json references accordingly.
Never test critical migrations only on devnet.
Run integration tests on testnet to reveal timing and ordering issues.
Key Takeaway

Match your test scope to the cluster: iteration on devnet, realistic testing on testnet, and audited releases on mainnet-beta.

screens.title: Anchor Deploy Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying an Anchor program is a repeatable process. First, ensure your Anchor. toml provider cluster points to the intended network and your wallet path points to the deployer keypair. Confirm the deployer wallet has sufficient SOL for the target cluster; devnet supports airdrops, whereas mainnet requires real funds. Next, from your program root run the anchor deploy command. Anchor will compile the Rust program, upload the program binary to the cluster, and print the new Program ID. A common error is assuming the Program ID will match a local validator. Instead, always copy the printed Program ID and update your Anchor. toml and target deploy artifacts. After deploy, update your client code to reference the new Program ID and test calls end-to-end. Concrete example: run anchor deploy --provider. cluster devnet to deploy to devnet and note the Program ID printed in the terminal output. Misconception: deploying once equals production-ready; it does not. You must audit, test, and secure keys before mainnet-beta deploys. Where could a deploy fail? Missing build dependencies, insufficient payer funds, or a misconfigured cluster setting — check logs and re-run after fixes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Anchor Deploy
Deploy Steps
  1. Set provider.cluster and wallet path in Anchor.toml.
  2. Ensure deployer wallet has SOL. On devnet use airdrop for quick funds.
  3. Run anchor deploy --provider.cluster devnet to build and deploy.
  4. Copy the Program ID printed after deploy and update your client and Anchor.toml.
  5. Verify transactions on a public explorer and test end-to-end flows.
Key Takeaway

Always capture the Program ID from the deploy output and update your client before testing.

Terminal Demo (Example)
# Deploy to devnet
anchor deploy --provider.cluster devnet

# Deploy to mainnet-beta (requires real SOL)
anchor deploy --provider.cluster mainnet-beta

# Sample output will include a Program ID you must copy:
# Program Id: 4xY...YourNewProgramIdHere
Note: If deploy fails, inspect compilation errors, missing crates, or payer balance.

screens.title: Update Client Configuration After Deploy
screens.narratorSegment: After a successful deploy you must wire your client to the correct program and cluster. The most common mistake is leaving a local Program ID or an incorrect endpoint, which can make your app appear broken or, worse, operate against the wrong network. Practically, open Anchor. toml and verify the programs table for the target cluster is updated with the new Program ID. Then, in your React client update the PROGRAM_ID constant to the new ID and set the ConnectionProvider network to WalletAdapterNetwork. Devnet or the appropriate cluster. A concrete example: after anchor deploy you will find target/deploy/counter-keypair. json updated; copy the Program ID string and paste it into src/FullCounterDApp. tsx. A misconception is that only the program binary changes; client-side ID references and IDL must also match the deployed program. Finally, test the UI fully: connect the wallet, run initialize and increment flows, and confirm transactions appear on the devnet explorer. If they don't, re-check endpoint, IDL version, and Program ID for mismatches. Update Client Configuration After Deploy means a correct program_id and endpoint are required for client interactions to reach the newly deployed program.. In practical terms, change program_id and endpoint so your dapp talks to the deployed program. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Client Update
Anchor.toml Snippet
[programs.devnet]
counter = "YOUR_NEW_DEVNET_PROGRAM_ID_HERE"

[provider]
cluster = "devnet"
wallet = "~/.config/solana/id.json"
Ensure the program entry is set for the correct cluster after deploy.
React client update
// Example constant in FullCounterDApp.tsx
export const PROGRAM_ID = new PublicKey('YOUR_NEW_DEVNET_PROGRAM_ID_HERE');

// Connection provider in App.tsx
const network = WalletAdapterNetwork.Devnet;
const endpoint = clusterApiUrl(network);
After editing, restart the app, connect wallet on devnet, and verify transactions.

screens.title: Key Management: Protecting Deploy & Upgrade Authority
screens.narratorSegment: Key management is the foundation of DApp security. Your program deployer key controls upgrades; if compromised, an attacker can replace your program with a malicious binary. Treat that key as a high-value secret. Best practices include storing the deployer key in an encrypted vault or on a hardware wallet and never committing keypair files like id. json to source control. If your deploy workflow requires automation, use short-lived or dedicated deployment keys kept in secure CI secrets and rotate them regularly. A concrete example: use a hardware wallet or an enterprise key vault to sign upgrade transactions, or move upgrade authority to a multi-signature wallet that requires multiple approvals. If a key is accidentally exposed, immediate steps are: generate a new keypair, perform an emergency upgrade using the new authority to either transfer upgrade authority to a multi-sig or make the program immutable, notify users, and audit transaction history. A common misconception is that only user wallets need hardware protection; in reality, any key that can modify programs or move funds should get the same safeguards. Final question to consider: have you mapped every key that can affect funds or upgrades and applied appropriate custody controls?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Key Management
Deployer Key
Used to deploy and, if allowed, to upgrade the on-chain program. Secure this key first.
Hardware Wallet / Vault
Prefer hardware devices or encrypted key vaults for any key that can modify program code or move funds.
Multi-sig Upgrade Authority
Reduce single-key risk by delegating upgrade authority to a multi-signature wallet.
Compromise Response
Rotate keys, emergency upgrade to remove upgrade authority or transfer to multi-sig, and notify users.
Practical Checklist
  • Never commit keypair files to Git.
  • Use CI secrets and ephemeral deploy keys for automation.
  • Prefer multi-sig for upgrade operations.
Common Mistake

Committing id.json to a repository exposes your deployer key and invites program hijacking.

screens.title: Reentrancy and Cross-Program Invocations
screens.narratorSegment: Let's dig into reentrancy on Solana and why the safe pattern is to update local state before calling other programs. Reentrancy is when a program's logic is re-entered by another instruction or CPI before the original state is finalized. Solana's runtime is single-threaded during transaction execution, which reduces some classical reentrancy risks. Yet cross-program invocations can still create windows where an external program can cause your program to behave unexpectedly. The reliable defense is simple: finalize and serialize your own state changes before performing any CPI that could allow control to jump to another program. For example, if you're moving funds out of an escrow PDA, first mark the escrow as closed or reduce its balance in your state, serialize that state, then invoke the token program to transfer tokens. A common misconception is that Solana's single-threaded model completely prevents reentrancy; it does not — the attacker can still craft a transaction sequence or CPI ordering that exploits an inconsistent state. Concrete example: in a marketplace, write the listing as inactive before transferring the NFT. Practice habitually using confirmed state updates first, then CPIs. Key takeaway: always make destructive or authoritative state changes durable before invoking external programs. Ask yourself: can an external program observe or act on my state mid-operation? If yes, reorder to protect the invariant.

content.html:
Core Concept

Reentrancy and Cross-Program Invocations

Make your state changes durable before calling other programs to avoid inconsistent invariants.
Why it matters
Attacks that exploit unfinished state can steal funds or corrupt program invariants.
Definition

Reentrancy occurs when execution control returns into a program at a point where its expected state was not yet finalized. On Solana, CPIs can create those return paths. Prevent this by writing state first, then calling other programs.

Pattern
  1. Validate inputs and signers.
  2. Update and serialize local state (mark closed, subtract balances).
  3. Perform CPIs such as token transfers.
  4. Emit logs and return success.
Common Mistake

Calling a token program to transfer before marking the source as spent. This leaves a window where a replayed CPI can act on stale state.

Concrete Example
// Pseudocode pattern // 1. mark escrow.closed = true // 2. serialize account data // 3. invoke token program to transfer escrow -> buyer // If steps reversed, buyer could trigger another transfer before state persists
Key Takeaway

Order state writes before CPIs to preserve invariants and block reentrancy-like exploits.

screens.title: Signer Spoofing vs. Ownership Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Signer spoofing and missing ownership checks are two distinct but related risks that lead to unauthorized actions in Solana programs. Signer spoofing happens when program logic assumes an account is a valid signer without verifying its actual authority or relationship to the resource. Missing ownership checks happen when a program operates on an account without confirming that the account's owner field equals the expected program ID. Both problems allow attackers to trick your program into modifying or moving assets. A practical contrast: signer spoofing affects who authorized the instruction; ownership checks protect whether a program is permitted to modify the account data. Use Anchor attributes like account signer validation, but also perform explicit logic checks such as comparing an account's owner to the expected program ID and asserting that account. owner == program_id when appropriate. Concrete example: if an instruction is meant to update a vault account owned by your program, check vault. owner equals your program's ID and verify the signer has the authority to request the change. A common misconception is relying only on the client to enforce permissions; on-chain programs must enforce them deterministically. End by asking yourself: who must sign and who must own each account? If that question isn't answered in code, add the checks now.

keyIdea.text: Signer flags and owner fields are separate protections; enforce both to prevent unauthorized actions.

content.html:
Comparison

Signer Spoofing vs. Ownership Checks

Both protect different axes of authority; you need both in program logic.
Signer Spoofing
When code assumes an account is authorized without verifying the signature or authority.
  • Symptoms: unexpected state changes after a transaction with unknown signers.
  • Mitigation: require is_signer checks and explicit authority fields in account data.
  • Example: check account.owner == expected_owner for role-based actions.
Misconception
Relying on client-side checks is ineffective; signature and authority must be validated on-chain.
Ownership Checks
Ensuring an account's owner field matches the program that should control it.
  • Symptoms: program modifies data in accounts owned by other programs.
  • Mitigation: assert account.owner == program_id when required.
  • Example: verify token account owner or PDA owner before state mutation.
Pro Tip
Combine owner checks with role fields stored inside the account for layered authorization.
Example Check
// Rust check
if account.owner != program_id { return Err(ProgramError::IncorrectProgramId); }
// Anchor-style authority
assert!(authority.key() == &profile.owner);

screens.title: Integer Overflow & Safe Arithmetic
screens.narratorSegment: Integer overflow and underflow are classic bugs with real monetary consequences. In debug builds Rust panics on overflow, but in release builds it will wrap by default. On Solana, wrapped arithmetic can silently change balances, counters, or reward calculations. The recommended pattern is to use checked arithmetic helpers: checked_add, checked_sub, and checked_mul. Each returns an Option that you can map into a program error on None. Anchor also offers a safe arithmetic feature or helper crates to make these checks ergonomic. A concrete example: when incrementing a u64 counter or adding tokens to a pooled balance, call checked_add and if it returns None, return an explicit arithmetic overflow error. A common misconception is that integer types are impossible to overflow in practical DeFi; in reality, attackers craft sequences that push values past limits. Here is a short Rust snippet you can use in a handler, where we read an account value, compute a new amount with checked_add, and serialize it back. Also log the before and after values for monitoring. End with the practical takeaway: never trust implicit wrapping — make arithmetic explicit and fail early so an error is visible in transaction logs.

keyIdea.title: Fail on overflow
keyIdea.text: Use checked arithmetic and explicit errors to prevent silent wrapping and fund loss.

content.html:
Definition

Integer Overflow & Safe Arithmetic

Protect numeric operations with checked arithmetic and explicit error handling.
Why it matters

A wrapped integer can turn a credit into a huge balance or make counters reset. Attackers and edge cases can exploit absent checks, so prefer checked arithmetic and return explicit errors.

Common Fix
let new = current.checked_add(amount).ok_or(ProgramError::Custom(0))?;
account.value = new;
account.serialize(&mut &mut acct.data.borrow_mut()[..])?;
Anchor & Safe Arithmetic

Anchor offers patterns and community crates to make checked math less noisy. When possible, centralize arithmetic checks in helper functions to keep instruction handlers readable.

Key Takeaway

Explicitly check arithmetic results and return clear errors to make failures diagnosable on-chain.

Concrete Code Example
// Example: safe increment
let mut data = Counter::try_from_slice(&acct.data.borrow())?;
let next = data.value.checked_add(1).ok_or(ProgramError::Custom(1))?;
data.value = next;
data.serialize(&mut &mut acct.data.borrow_mut()[..])?;

screens.title: Front-running, Sandwich Attacks & Denial of Service
screens.narratorSegment: Front-running and sandwich attacks exploit transaction ordering and mempool visibility. On Solana, validators and bots can observe pending transactions and submit competing transactions to profit from price movements or to manipulate ordering. While you cannot fully eliminate this visibility, you can design program-level mitigations: minimize on-chain dependency on user-supplied order-sensitive data, use time-based locks or nonces, collapse multiple steps into atomic instructions, and avoid predictable state transitions that expose arbitrage. Sandwich attacks typically target AMM-like swaps; consider slippage limits, minimum acceptable outputs, and on-chain order matching patterns that reduce on-chain price exposure. Denial of Service attacks often come from spamming invalid or expensive instructions; mitigate by adding cheap pre-flight validation that fails fast, requiring small deposits for expensive actions, or limiting per-account rate. A practical design pattern: validate input ranges and signer permissions first, then perform cheap checks before any expensive state or compute steps. Also include monitoring and alerting so you detect spikes in failed or pending transactions. A misconception is that program-level checks alone stop bots; they reduce the profitable surface but must be combined with off-chain rate limits and economic disincentives. Conclude by asking: what costly path can an attacker trigger and how can you detect and throttle it?

keyIdea.title: Limit exploitability
keyIdea.text: Design atomic instructions, validate fast, and use economic or time-based throttles to reduce front-running and DoS risk.

content.html:
Process Flow

Front-running, Sandwich & DoS Mitigations

A mix of atomic design, fast validation, and economic controls reduce these attacks.
Step 1 — Validate Fast

Perform cheap, decisive checks early: signatures, rent-exemption, and input bounds. Fail early to avoid wasted compute and exploitable windows.

Step 2 — Atomicize Operations

Design instructions so a single transaction completes a logical unit. Avoid multi-transaction state transitions that expose intermediate states to bots.

Step 3 — Economic Controls

Use slippage limits, deposits, or fees to make attacks costly. Rate-limit per-account actions with timestamped counters.

Concrete Example

For a swap: require a maximum slippage parameter signed by the user, compute price impact, and fail if the impact exceeds the signed slippage. This ensures a bot cannot slip the trade beyond the user’s expectation.

Monitoring

Track pending transaction spikes, repeated failures, and unusual mempool activity. Alert on sudden fee increases or many rejects.

Key Takeaway

Combine fast validation, atomic design, and economic disincentives to reduce front-running and DoS vectors.

screens.title: Preparing for Public Release
screens.narratorSegment: Shipping a DApp to mainnet-beta is an orchestration problem: code, keys, monitoring, and communication must all be ready. Start by engaging a professional smart contract audit to discover logic flaws, missing checks, and gas or compute inefficiencies. Auditors provide remediation guidance but you should also run thorough internal tests and a public bug bounty. For monitoring, set up RPC and indexer analytics to track transaction volume, error rates, and gas spikes. Configure alerts for unusual patterns such as repeated failed instructions or sudden balance changes in PDAs. Documentation is essential: publish clear user guidance, explain known limitations, and warn about irreversible operations. For rollout, prefer a phased approach: a small beta on testnet, a limited mainnet soft launch to a whitelist, then full open release. Finally, prepare emergency procedures: maintain a secure upgrade authority in a hardware wallet or multi-sig, have scripts and prebuilt upgrades to pause or fix functionality, and define communication templates to notify users quickly. A common misconception is that an upgrade authority alone is enough; it's safer to use a multi-sig or procedures that rotate authority and minimize single-key risk. End with this question: do you have monitoring and a rehearsed emergency playbook to act within minutes when an incident happens?

keyIdea.title: Plan the whole release
keyIdea.text: Combine audits, monitoring, clear docs, phased rollout, and rehearsed emergency steps to protect users and reputation.

content.html:
Release Checklist

Prepare your DApp for public release

Auditing, monitoring, docs, rollout, and emergency plans are essential for mainnet readiness.
Auditing

Hire professional auditors. Follow up with fixes, re-audits if needed, and publish a changelog of fixes for transparency.

Monitoring

Track transaction rates, errors, PDA balance changes, and unusual latency. Alert on anomalies and retain logs for forensics.

Documentation

Provide end‑user docs, developer integration notes, and security disclaimers. Clear docs reduce support load and user errors.

Rollout Strategy

Use staged releases: testnet beta, small mainnet soft launches, then full public release. Collect metrics and feedback at each stage.

Emergency Procedures
  • Maintain upgrade authority in a hardware wallet or multi-sig.
  • Prepare rollback or pause upgrades and tested scripts.
  • Have a communication plan for users and stakeholders.
Final Checklist

Audit complete, monitoring live, docs published, phased rollout planned, and emergency playbook rehearsed — only then consider mainnet-beta deployment.

What to Remember

Key Concepts

Three compact reminders to carry into every deployment.
Key Management
Keep deployer and upgrade keys secure, prefer hardware wallets or multi-sig and never commit keys to Git.

Safe Arithmetic
Use checked_add, checked_sub, and explicit errors. Avoid silent wrapping in release builds.
Summary Takeaway

Secure keys, verify ownership and signer authority, and make arithmetic explicit. These three guardrails prevent the most damaging deployment mistakes.

Additional Essentials

Authority management, audits, monitoring, and an emergency playbook complete your readiness checklist.

Deployment is more than making code available; it's about releasing a reliable, secure application that interacts with real value. In this lesson you will learn how to move your Anchor program through devnet and testnet into mainnet-beta, how to update client configuration after a deploy, and how to protect the keys that control upgrades and ownership. We will emphasize practical steps: running anchor deploy, noting the new Program ID, updating the client PROGRAM_ID and connection endpoint, and validating behavior on a public explorer. Security is threaded through every step. You will see concrete recommendations for storing deployer keys, preferring hardware wallets or encrypted vaults, and the immediate actions to take if a key is exposed. Finally, we'll preview common vulnerabilities you must check for — reentrancy-like flows, signer and ownership checks, integer wrapping, and denial-of-service vectors — and how to adopt simple defensive patterns. By the end of the section you'll understand the deploy lifecycle and why careful key management and auditing are essential before going live.

These objectives map directly to the practical steps and security practices you'll apply. First, you will deploy Anchor programs to the public Solana clusters: devnet for rapid iteration, testnet for larger-scale integration, and mainnet-beta for production. You will practice updating the client PROGRAM_ID and endpoint after deploy so your DApp points to the correct cluster. Second, you will learn key management strategies: protecting the deployer private key, using encrypted vaults or hardware wallets, and what to do if a key is exposed. Third, you'll implement common security patterns inside your programs: ownership checks, signer verification, checked arithmetic, and careful mutability declarations. Finally, you'll prepare a DApp for release by planning audit engagements, setting up monitoring, and defining emergency procedures such as upgrade authority rotation or pausing functionality. Each objective pairs a practical task with the reason it matters in production, so you can both act and explain the risk to your team.

This second objectives slide highlights concrete skills and safeguards you must practice. First, you will learn to update client configuration after every deploy — setting the PROGRAM_ID in your client and confirming the RPC endpoint matches the deployed cluster. This small step prevents accidental mainnet interactions when you expect devnet. Second, you'll build judgment about mutability and account ownership; only mark accounts mutable when necessary and always verify account. owner equals your program ID. Third, you will be able to recognize deployment anti-patterns, such as committing id. json to version control or leaving an upgrade authority single-signed. Finally, you will prepare a monitoring and incident response plan: choose on-chain monitoring tools, log key events, and decide an emergency upgrade or pause strategy. Each card links a practical action to why it reduces risk, so you graduate able to act and to explain those actions during a release or incident.

Understanding the three public Solana clusters is essential to a safe deploy process. Devnet is the development playground: you can airdrop free SOL, iterate quickly, and accept that state can reset. Use it for daily development, quick client integration, and early user flows. Testnet is a more stable public network that better mirrors mainnet-beta behavior and uptime; use it for larger integration tests and load scenarios before a public release. Mainnet-beta is the production network where real value moves. Deploys here must be audited, your deployer key must be secured, and rollback or emergency plans should be ready. A common misconception is treating devnet tests as sufficient for production; devnet does not guarantee the same uptime or network conditions. Another subtle point: program IDs created by a local validator will differ from the ID produced by anchor deploy to a public cluster, so always note the Program ID printed after deploy and update your client. Example: you will typically develop and test on devnet, then run broader tests on testnet, and finally perform a controlled, phased roll-out to mainnet-beta. Ask yourself: have I tested scale and secured upgrade paths before mainnet?

Confirm the deployer wallet has sufficient SOL for the target cluster; devnet supports airdrops, whereas mainnet requires real funds. Next, from your program root run the anchor deploy command. Anchor will compile the Rust program, upload the program binary to the cluster, and print the new Program ID. A common error is assuming the Program ID will match a local validator. Instead, always copy the printed Program ID and update your Anchor. toml and target deploy artifacts. After deploy, update your client code to reference the new Program ID and test calls end-to-end. Concrete example: run anchor deploy --provider. cluster devnet to deploy to devnet and note the Program ID printed in the terminal output. Misconception: deploying once equals production-ready; it does not. You must audit, test, and secure keys before mainnet-beta deploys. Where could a deploy fail? Missing build dependencies, insufficient payer funds, or a misconfigured cluster setting — check logs and re-run after fixes.

After a successful deploy you must wire your client to the correct program and cluster. The most common mistake is leaving a local Program ID or an incorrect endpoint, which can make your app appear broken or, worse, operate against the wrong network.
